description: WQ-443 control registry. Every step in pack/scripts/verify-audit-behavior.ps1 appears here exactly once. Read by the coverage guard inside that suite and by pack/scripts/verify-guard-proofs.ps1. Plan: docs/GUARD_PROOF_PLAN.md
_comment_statusVocabulary: There is deliberately no 'proven' status. A proof is a run outcome, not a fact a file can hold - a stored 'proven' becomes a stale claim the first time nobody runs the runner, which is exactly the inert-but-authoritative artifact WQ-460 removed. This file holds the specification; verify-guard-proofs.ps1 produces the proof.

statusVocabulary.mutation: Carries a spec the runner can apply. Three actions: the default 'replace' (file, find, replace) edits text that must occur exactly once; 'create' (file, action, content) writes a file the tree does not have; 'delete' (file, action) removes one it does. The last two exist because a guard whose subject is a file's presence or absence cannot be broken by editing text. Every step named in expectFailIn must report [FAIL] once it is applied, and the run is what proves it.
statusVocabulary.exempt: No executable spec. Requires a reason from reasonVocabulary.

reasonVocabulary.grandfathered-pre-wq443: Predates the registry. CLOSED - not permitted on any step added after schema 1 shipped. Retrofit is tracked as its own queue row, not closed by this file.
reasonVocabulary.not-applicable: The step cannot meaningfully be made to fail by mutating the pack. Requires justification in note, and is the only reason available to a new step that is not proven.

_comment_exemptSteps: WQ-467: which steps are exempt, named rather than counted. Three rows once changed from exempt to a full mutation spec inside an hour with no edit anyone could account for - the specs were sound and were later proven by execution, so what went unexplained was the transition, and nothing in the system disagreed with it. Step 71 printed the counts every run, and a printed count nobody recorded is a number, not a check. Steps are named rather than totalled because a count cannot see a swap: one row retrofitted while another regresses keeps the total intact. Keep this list in the same edit as the status it describes; that edit is the explanation the incident lacked.
_comment_schemaSealedAtStep: The highest step number that existed when this registry was seeded. A closed reason is only valid at or below the seal, which is what makes grandfathering unusable for a new step - the seal is a number, not a promise. Raising it is how the discipline would be quietly abandoned, so behavior step 71 asserts the value and the changelog records any change.

steps.title: audit_code_checks.py --self-test

mutation.why: Adds a module to the self-test's expected domain map for section F that the fixture never contained, so the engine's own proof reports parse_domain_map returning less than it should and exits 1. That is how this breaks in practice - a fixture and the assertion over it drift apart, and the self-test is the only thing that says so. The subject of this step is whether the suite notices that the engine's proof failed, not whether the parser works.
mutation.rejected: Breaking parse_domain_map itself was rejected: it reddens most of the suite and proves only that everything downstream depends on it. Batch eighteen ran this same spec and could not record the result - the self-test printed its finding to stderr, PowerShell made that a NativeCommandError, and the runner's own Stop preference turned it terminating (WQ-475), so the proof died at the invoke line with no results file. That is fixed in this release, which is the only reason this step is provable at all.

steps.note: Collateral is wide and entirely expected: steps 21, 22, 23, 43 and 54 failed alongside on a green baseline, all of them steps that run the engine's self-test as a gate rather than as their subject - run_audit_core.ps1 raises a Fix from it and check-requirements.ps1 treats it as a required preflight result. A narrower mutation is not available and would not be better: the self-test is a single pass/fail signal, so anything that reddens this step reddens every consumer of it. Attribution stays clean because the mutation is one literal in one set in one test.

steps.title: Fixture JSON + manifest sections F and K

mutation.why: Lowercases the section key on the way into the domain map, whose keys are the uppercase section letters, so every lookup misses and each section's module list arrives empty. The manifest is what tells an agent which modules a section covers, so a section reports a complete review of a scope it was never given - and the row still exists, with the right letter and the right shape, which is why this reads as working code. A case mismatch on dictionary keys is the ordinary way this happens.
mutation.rejected: Dropping the multi-module row from requiredSections was rejected because audit_code_checks.py --self-test asserts that letter directly, and step 1 runs first: the suite would abort before reaching step 2 and the runner could only report that no results file was written.

steps.note: The witness is the multi-module arm, which names the missing module rather than the empty list. Collateral is plausible here rather than ruled out: steps 11 and 12 read the same manifest, and if either asserts on modules it will fail alongside - attributable either way, since the mutated lookup is one expression in one function. Confirmed on a green baseline in a lane of its own: no collateral, and steps 11 and 12 stayed green, so the empty module list is visible only where the manifest row is asserted.

steps.title: run_audit_core.ps1 -SkipTests must exit 1

mutation.why: Stops a tests-skipped run from raising the incomplete-audit fix. The exit code is derived from the fix count, so a -SkipTests audit would then exit 0 and read as a completed audit - the loophole the rules and the skill both spend paragraphs forbidding.

steps.note: Mutating the fix that a skipped-tests run raises, rather than the exit statement, because the exit code is only a consequence of the fix list. A mutation of the exit line would leave the report saying the audit was incomplete while the code said it passed, which is a different defect from the one this step guards. Expect step 14 as collateral - it asserts the same fix reaches the manifest's gate list, so the two cannot be separated by any mutation of the fix itself.

steps.title: Template hygiene

mutation.content:
# Orphan duplicate audit template

Planted by the guard-proof runner. This is the defect step 4 exists to catch: a second audit
template at the templates root, which drifts from the one under templates/docs until two projects
bootstrapped a month apart disagree about what the checklist says.
mutation.why: The subject of this step is an absence, so nothing the runner could edit reaches it - which is why the step stayed exempt through eighteen batches while its spec was trivially writable. The create action exists for this shape and step 7's mirror of it.
mutation.rejected: Editing the surviving template under templates/docs was rejected: it would prove that some other guard reads that file, and say nothing about whether this one notices a duplicate.

steps.note: First use of the create action (2.22.113). Collateral on a green baseline: steps 5 and 23, both for the same reason the orphan is a defect - it is in no manifest list, so the sync-tracking arm and the generated-project audit report an untracked template alongside.

steps.title: Rules and skill one-standard text

mutation.find: Gate-only is forbidden. Gaps = Fix or Improve only.
mutation.replace: Gate-only is forbidden, except that a debug audit script may run machine checks only. Gaps = Fix or Improve only.
mutation.why: Plants the loophole this step exists to keep out. The skill is what an agent reads before auditing, so a sentence permitting machine checks only is not documentation drift - it is the instruction, and an audit that skips the tests is the failure mode the whole one-standard rule was written for. The exemption is phrased the way a real one would be: narrow, reasonable, and applying to exactly the case where someone is in a hurry.
mutation.rejected: Removing the prohibition sentence instead would fail the positive arm, and was the candidate reconnaissance preferred. Planting the loophole is better for the same reason step 61 needed a planted construct: this arm expects zero findings from a text scan, and a scan that finds nothing looks identical whether the file is clean or the check is blind. The prohibition token appears exactly once in this file, so removal was available - it just proves less.

steps.note: Two files are scanned in the same loop, the skill and pack/rules/audit-protocol.mdc, and the mutation lands in the skill so the message names which one. Nothing else in the suite reads this skill, so no collateral is expected. Note that the same step number also carries the manifest-coverage arms, which are the expensive part deferred through sixteen batches; those remain unproven and this proof does not claim them.

steps.title: Config template hygiene

mutation.why: Puts the retired key back into the config every generated project starts from. It was removed because it let a project run a subset of its tests and still call the audit complete - and shipping it in the template means every new project inherits the loophole in its own config, where a later fix to the pack default cannot reach it. The same shape as WQ-452: four places carried that assumption and fixing only the code default left every project pinned.

steps.note: The key appears nowhere functional any more - only in this step and in the changelog entry recording its removal - so the mutation cannot reach another guard.

steps.title: Agent workflow docs

mutation.why: Three of this step's four arms assert that a file is present, and the fourth reads text out of this one, so removing it is the regression the step describes: a doc renamed or moved while every rule that cites it keeps pointing at the old path. A delete is also the only mutation that reaches an existence check at all.
mutation.rejected: Rewording the loop-back phrase was rejected on a measurement rather than on taste: 'all projects' occurs twice in this doc, and a find that matches twice is refused by design, so the spec would have had to quote nine lines of prose and would go stale on the next edit to any of them.

steps.note: Collateral on a green baseline: steps 23, 47 and 52, all of them consumers rather than subjects - the manifest lists this doc, so the cited-files, export and generated-project checks report it missing alongside. Attribution stays clean because step 7 is the only one whose subject it is.

steps.title: Semantic report verify

mutation.why: Stubs out the test-pass proof head, which is the value that ties a semantic report to the test run it describes. With no head there is nothing to compare, so a report written against an older tree can never be found stale - the freshness gate stops being a gate. A stubbed return is the shape of a debugging leftover, and it is invisible in review because the call it replaces is on the line above in every diff.
mutation.rejected: Weakening --verify-semantic-report itself was rejected because this step's fixture is valid: the verify is expected to exit 0, so a more permissive verify keeps the step green and proves nothing. Only the arms that require a value - proof head, template written, fill succeeded - can witness a defect here.

steps.note: Steps 9 and 10 also ask for the proof head but do not require it to be non-empty, so they proceed with an empty value in the manifest stub and stay green. That asymmetry is the reason this target is attributable at all.

steps.title: Semantic cite validation

mutation.why: Flips the default to cites-optional, so 'problem found with no cite' is accepted as a reviewed section. That is the loophole the requirement exists to close: a report can claim a finding in prose while naming no file, and a later reader cannot tell whether the section was reviewed or narrated. The default is the target because a project that never sets the key is every project using the template unmodified.
mutation.rejected: Mutating `summary_has_cite` to `return True` looks more direct and is useless here: audit_code_checks.py --self-test asserts that predicate directly, so step 1 fails first, the suite aborts before writing results, and the runner reports 'no results file' rather than anything about step 9. A mutation has to survive the checks upstream of the step it is aiming at.

steps.note: Permissive by direction: under the mutation validation accepts more, so collateral would have to come from another step that asserts a *rejection*. The pack's own report carries real cites, so its verify is unaffected.
steps.foundDefect: The mutation left the suite green, because the step was passing for reasons it did not name. Its fixture omitted modulesReviewed[], which is required for sections D-K, and gave section D a lone 'command' evidence item, which also trips the file/test requirement when not clean - so the verify had two other grounds to reject and would have rejected with cite checking switched off entirely. The fixture now supplies modulesReviewed and valid file evidence, leaving the missing cite as the only defect, and the step asserts the rejection message mentions the cite.

steps.title: Semantic evidence validation

mutation.why: Drops the required evidence count to zero by default, restoring the state before evidence was mandatory: a section may report a real finding with an empty evidence array, so the claim is unverifiable by anyone who did not watch the review happen. The default is the right target because a project that never sets the key - which is every project using the template unmodified - is exactly who this protects.

steps.note: Chosen over inverting `not clean` because that inversion would demand evidence for every 'Nothing found.' section, which the pack's own report has by the dozen - the whole verify would collapse and the proof would say nothing about this step. Lowering the default touches only the not-clean branch.
steps.foundDefect: The mutation left the suite green, because the step was passing for a reason it did not name: modulesReviewed[] is required for sections D-K, the fixture omitted it, and the verify was rejecting the report over that rather than over the empty evidence array. The fixture now supplies modulesReviewed and the step asserts the rejection message mentions evidence, so a disabled evidence minimum can no longer hide behind an unrelated rejection.

steps.title: machineCoverage completeness

mutation.why: Blanks the per-section count of machine checks while leaving the coverage map populated. That is the shape of a real refactor loss: the manifest still lists sections and still looks complete, so an agent reading it cannot tell that a section has zero machine checks behind it and needs the deeper semantic pass. A null that renders as empty is worse than a missing key, which would at least raise.

steps.note: The count is what makes coverage actionable - the map alone says a section was considered, not how much of it a machine actually checked.
steps.collateral: Step 2 also fails, and that is correct rather than noise: it reads the same manifest and asserts sections F and K arrive complete, so a blanked count is a real defect from where it is standing too. A narrower mutation would have to single out one section by letter, which is not a shape any refactor produces.

steps.title: Semantic vs machine alignment

mutation.why: Negates the alignment test, so a section may report 'Nothing found.' while machine checks hold open issues for it - and a section that honestly describes those issues gets reported instead. This is the check that stops a semantic review from contradicting the machine half of the same audit, which is the one contradiction a reader has no way to detect from the report alone.

steps.note: A negation slip rather than a disabled branch: `if False` would prove the same step and describe a defect nobody writes. The inversion also keeps the check running and reporting, which is the harder failure to notice.
steps.foundDefect: The mutation left the suite green. The fixture removed hardware_cache.py from section F's modulesReviewed[] as well as from disk, and the omission raises its own 'modulesReviewed missing' fix - so the verify was rejecting the report over coverage and would have kept rejecting it with the alignment test negated. Reproducing the fixture by hand showed eleven other fixes in the same output. modulesReviewed now keeps the module, which is also the truer fixture: the expanded domain map is built from config rather than disk, so a section listing a deleted module is exactly the contradiction under test - it claims to have reviewed what the machine reports missing. The step now asserts the rejection quotes "cannot be 'Nothing found.'".

steps.title: Section L gitignore audit artifacts

mutation.find: if not found and norm not in combined.replace("\\", "/"):
mutation.replace: if found and norm not in combined.replace("\\", "/"):
mutation.why: Inverts the report condition, so a .gitignore that is missing an audit artifact passes and one that lists it is reported instead. Chosen over emptying the default list because an empty list is a visibly broken config, while an inverted test looks like a working check right up to the point where a manifest full of machine paths gets committed.

steps.note: Low collateral by construction: under the mutation the check reports fewer real gaps, so other steps and generated-project audits lose a fix rather than gain one.

steps.title: The shipped POSIX surface avoids what macOS does not have (WQ-455)

mutation.why: Makes every detector report nothing, so a shell script calling sha256sum or declare -A passes as portable. That is the state this step was added from: the macOS surface unverified, with no Mac available to find out. A silent detector is the right defect to recreate, because the check would still run, still print, and still say the surface is clean.

steps.note: The positive cases are the point: a detector nobody has watched fire is a detector nobody has tested, and this step exists precisely because the hardware that would otherwise catch these is unavailable. The first control guards the opposite failure - a check that flags portable code gets muted, and a muted check is worse than none.

steps.title: auditGateFixes manifest (Incomplete audit not in Section L)

mutation.find: if ($f -match '^Semantic report missing|^Semantic report invalid|^Semantic report verify failed|^Incomplete audit') {
mutation.replace: if ($f -match '^Semantic report missing|^Semantic report invalid|^Semantic report verify failed') {
mutation.why: Stops 'Incomplete audit' from being recognised as a gate fix, so it drops out of auditGateFixes and falls through into the per-section mapping instead. Both halves are the defect this step is named for: an agent reading auditGateFixes sees a complete audit, and the gate condition reappears as though some section owned it - Section L historically, which made a whole-audit problem look like one checklist item somebody could tick off.

steps.note: Distinct from step 3, which asserts audit_code_checks.py *raises* the incomplete-audit fix. This step asserts run_audit_core.ps1 files it in the right channel afterwards - raising it and then misfiling it is a separate failure, and mutating the recogniser separates the two cleanly.

steps.title: Semantic gate fix patterns (not Section L wiring)

mutation.find: if ($f -match 'Audit sync|Audit wiring|Code checks|Missing audit file|Old audit|forbidden rule|Forbidden') {
mutation.replace: if ($f -match 'Semantic report|Audit sync|Audit wiring|Code checks|Missing audit file|Old audit|forbidden rule|Forbidden') {
mutation.why: Widens the Section L wiring bucket until it also claims the gate messages the engine emits, which is precisely what this step's title says must not happen. Runtime output does not change - the gate branch above returns first - so the only thing that notices is the step whose subject this is.
mutation.rejected: Rewording the engine's message was rejected because the step would then stop recognising it as a gate message at all and would report nothing; a mutation has to break the invariant, not remove one side of it from view.

steps.note: The step was rewritten in the same release (2.22.113) before it could be proven. It previously matched four sample strings, written out eight lines above, against two regexes also written out there - no mutation of the pack could have made it fail, and it had passed unchanged through every rewording of the messages it claimed to check. It now reads the classifier out of run_audit_core.ps1 and the messages out of audit_code_checks.py, so it fails when those two disagree.

steps.title: FinalizeOnly blocked without prior test pass

mutation.why: Trusts the mode instead of the proof, so -FinalizeOnly certifies a project whose tests were never run - or were run against a different tree. Finalize is the step that stamps the audit as complete, so the whole gate reduces to whichever switch the caller passed.

steps.note: Rejected once before it was proven: the mutation left the step green because the run still exited non-zero over the incomplete semantic report, and the message assertion was 'test|proof|manifest' - three words ordinary audit output contains. WQ-466 gave this step a message check; it did not check that the message was specific. The assertion now looks for 'Audit finalize blocked', which only Test-ManifestFinalizeAllowed emits. Steps 17 and 23 go red alongside it, and that is the blast radius rather than noise: the bypassed function is also what loads testsGitHead and testsPassedAt out of the manifest, so a finalize that stops checking the proof also stops preserving it, and a generated project's own audit inherits both.

steps.title: FinalizeOnly preserves manifest test-pass proof

mutation.why: Writes the timestamp into the field that holds the test-pass proof - the copy-paste slip between two adjacent Add-Member lines, which is what makes it realistic. The proof is how a finalize pass knows the tests it is finalizing are the tests that ran against this tree; replaced by a timestamp, it can never match a recomputed head, so the pairing silently stops being checkable while both fields still look populated.
mutation.rejected: Wrapping the value in a conditional on FinalizeOnly was proposed and rejected as unrealistic - nobody ships a guard clause that blanks a field only on one code path. A field typo between neighbouring lines is a mistake that survives review.

steps.note: The witnessing arm compares the value after finalize against the value pass 1 recorded and prints what it got, so the failure names the timestamp sitting where a head belongs. Collateral is expected in steps that read the same proof field - step 18's finalize path and step 23's git-backed arm, which asserts the proof is commit-plus-content.

steps.title: Auditor workflow E2E - pass 1, semantic, finalize exit 0

mutation.why: Inverts the semantic gate's reviewed test, so a fully reviewed report is refused and a report nobody read is accepted. This step is the only one that walks the whole auditor path - write the template, fill every section, finalize - and a gate that can never be satisfied stops it at the last move while leaving the earlier passes intact.
mutation.rejected: Breaking the finalize entry point itself was rejected: it fails this step by never reaching the gate, which proves the script runs rather than that the workflow completes.

steps.note: Collateral on a green baseline: steps 8, 9, 10 and 23, which is every other step that fills a semantic report and expects it to verify. The inversion is one token in one condition, so nothing else in the engine changes shape.

steps.title: Audit phase timing log

mutation.why: A guard that requires the map to be non-empty before writing the first entry can never write anything, so every run logs "phases": {} and the audit keeps reporting a total with no breakdown. The log still appears, still parses, and still carries totalSeconds - which is exactly why the original assertion missed it.

steps.note: Retrofitting this step found the assertion was unable to fail this way: `-not $tl.phases` is false for an empty JSON object, because ConvertFrom-Json returns an object with no properties rather than $null. The step now counts the properties, and the mutation above is what proves the count is load-bearing.

steps.title: Mirror direction - source pack wins, installed copy never writes back

mutation.why: Reverses the default mirror direction, so a machine-local installed copy overwrites the source pack. That is the failure the direction rule exists to prevent, and it is silent: the sync reports success while quietly moving edits the wrong way, and on a removable source pack the loss is unrecoverable because this checkout keeps no version control.

steps.note: The four-space indent matters: the same call appears inside a one-line if on the preceding branch, and a spec matching twice is rejected.

steps.title: Requirements preflight

mutation.why: Promotes git from optional to required, which contradicts the decision WQ-459 settled: version control is optional to this pack, and a download, a zip, a folder copy and a flash drive are all supported deliveries. A required git tells a first-time user on any of those that the audit engine cannot run, when the only thing they lose is a git-HEAD fingerprint in place of a file-tree one - and it would declare this very checkout unfit, since it keeps no repository at all. One boolean, in the branch that runs whenever git is present, so the preflight still exits 0 and still reports ok: nothing looks wrong except the column that says whether the user has to act.
mutation.rejected: Breaking the Python probe so the preflight exits non-zero was rejected: it proves the gate rather than the required-versus-optional split, and several steps downstream depend on this preflight passing, so the failure would spread to steps that say nothing about requirements.

steps.note: One arm is the witness, by construction: git is on PATH on any machine running the suite, so the ok branch is the live one, the aggregate stays ok, and the exit code does not move - only 'required vs optional split (git and mcp optional)' can see it. Step 41 also reads this script and is unaffected, because it asserts the presence of the cross-platform gates by text rather than any requirement's flag.

steps.title: Pack tests run without pytest

mutation.why: Drops the flag that runs the behavior suite on both PowerShell hosts. Half the coverage disappears and every run still reports OK, which matters more here than in most projects: 5.1-versus-7 divergence is a defect class this pack has shipped before - a BOM on one host, -Include matching 3723 files on one and 4 on the other - and it is invisible unless both hosts actually execute. Removing a flag to make the suite finish sooner is the most ordinary way this protection is lost.
mutation.rejected: Inverting the exit code in tests/test_pack_audit.py was the other candidate and is weaker: it fails the run arm, which is an exit-code assertion, while this target fails the delegation arm on its own named message about losing both-host coverage.

steps.note: The static arm greps the implementation rather than running it, so the mutation costs nothing at runtime and no other step reads this file. The run arm keeps passing, correctly - the unit tests still work, which is exactly the state that makes lost host coverage hard to notice.

steps.title: Bootstrap smoke - a generated project audits itself

mutation.why: Renames one key in the substitution map without touching the templates that use it, so every generated file keeps the raw placeholder. That is not a hypothetical shape - a project once shipped with a literal placeholder in the title of its handoff README because one writer plain-copied where the others substituted - and this step is what stands between that and a user's new project.
mutation.rejected: Breaking the generated audit entry point was rejected: it reddens this step through a crash rather than through the generator handing the user a half-finished file, and the crash arm is already reachable from several other mutations.

steps.note: This step generates four projects and audits each of them, so it is the slowest in the suite; that is a reason to keep the mutation narrow, not a reason to leave it unproven. Nothing outside bootstrap reads this map.

steps.title: Executed code is ASCII and BOM-free

mutation.find: """Domain map lists modules - verify each concrete *.py exists on disk."""
mutation.replace: """Domain map lists modules — verify each concrete *.py exists on disk."""
mutation.why: Puts an em dash in a docstring of a file that runs, which is the exact character behind three separate failures: PowerShell 5.1 reads a BOM-less file as ANSI and turned an em dash into a stray quote that broke parsing, and a generated project's tests died printing one to a cp1252 console. A docstring is the right site because it is the place an author is most likely to type real typography without thinking of it as code.

steps.note: Written as \u2014 so this registry file stays ASCII itself. The runner unescapes on read, so the mutated copy carries the real character - a literal em dash here would make the control file an instance of what it is testing for.

steps.title: Fixture filler refuses outside the harness

mutation.why: Turns the opt-in into a test almost nothing satisfies, so --fill-semantic-fixture-test runs for any caller. That flag marks every checklist section reviewed with no findings and fills the counts the semantic gate cross-checks, which makes it a one-command way to fake an audit - and it ships in every install.

steps.note: The suite sets AUDIT_FIXTURE_TEST=1 for its own fixtures, so a mutation that only widens the gate leaves every other step working normally. That is the danger the step exists for: nothing breaks when this guard goes, which is why it needs a test rather than a code comment.

steps.title: Installer profile writes (MCP merge + copy filter)

mutation.why: Drops the negation from the test that adds an empty server map only when the file lacks one, so a config that *does* have servers gets that map overwritten with an empty one and every server the user configured is gone after the install writes the file back. This is the original defect's symptom restored exactly - the installer once kept only agent-hygiene and destroyed the rest - and it is the worst class of bug this pack can ship, because it happens during an install, to a file the pack does not own, on a machine where the user's other MCP servers are the reason the config exists.
mutation.rejected: Replacing the Add-Member registration with the dot-assignment that caused the original incident was rejected as the less precise mutation: the assignment throws on a PSCustomObject from ConvertFrom-Json, and the throw escapes to the step's own catch, so the step fails through 'installer probe error' rather than through the arm that counts surviving servers. A sign error that keeps the function running proves the arm; an exception proves the try block.

steps.note: The first arm names it precisely - 'MCP merge kept 1 of 3 servers - pre-existing servers destroyed' - and the BOM arm keeps passing, correctly, since the write path is untouched. No collateral is expected: install.ps1 is the one script the suite cannot run for real, so its functions reach the suite only through the AST extraction this step performs, and no other step extracts Merge-McpJson.

steps.title: Agent context refresh (stamp, change detection, pack vs app brief)
steps.note: Two arms are the witnesses and both were built as a matched pair - a negative control on alwaysApply:false and a positive control on a rule arriving in the load path - which is why an inversion cannot hide here. Step 54 also runs this script through the shell wrapper but asserts only that a context file was written, so it stays green. Steps 52 and 54 also reported failures. Collateral observed in this run was measured under four concurrent prover lanes, and steps 52 and 23 fail there from file-sharing contention in the export and bootstrap probes rather than from any mutation - the same contention failed one lane's baseline outright. Their appearance below is therefore unverified as collateral, not confirmed as it. Filed as WQ-474. The claim above that step 54 stays green is what this run could not confirm; it needs one uncontended lane to settle.

mutation.why: Inverts the front-matter test that decides whether a rule is always-on, which is the single question WQ-456 was about: a rule can be present, correct and never loaded, and months of work went missing that way. Under the mutation an always-on rule in the load path is reported as not loaded, and a rule explicitly marked alwaysApply:false is counted as loaded - so the brief tells an agent the opposite of what its editor will do, in both directions.
mutation.rejected: Renaming the firstRefresh marker was rejected as too cheap: it fails a labelling arm with no consequence for a reader, while the rule-load verdict is the part of this brief an agent acts on.

steps.title: Layout hygiene reports Improve, not delete-only Fix

mutation.find: Add-LayoutImprove "Layout - duplicate stable copy in repo
mutation.replace: Add-LayoutFix "Layout - duplicate stable copy in repo
mutation.why: Routes a layout finding into Fix, which is the state Section B was in before this step existed: a delete list an agent can close by deleting, without ever judging whether the tree is comprehensible. Add-LayoutFix is a real function in the same file, so this is a one-word slip a reviewer would read straight past.

steps.note: Only the channel assertion moves. Add-LayoutFix still records the line in $script:LayoutImproves, so the manifest arm and the glossary/duplicate/ephemeral reporting arm both stay green - the mutation isolates the Improve-vs-Fix claim rather than knocking the whole step over.

steps.title: Cross-version parity (PowerShell 5.1 vs 7)

mutation.why: Turns the version floor into a comment. The directive is what stops Windows PowerShell from starting a script that needs 7, failing in the middle of an audit instead of at the door; as prose it enforces nothing and still reads as documented. This is a tidying edit, which is why it is the realistic one - nobody deletes a floor on purpose.
mutation.rejected: Making the shared BOM-free writer emit a BOM was rejected on blast radius: it fails the parity probe convincingly but takes every BOM-sensitive step with it, and a mutation whose collateral is that wide cannot say which promise it broke.

It confirms this step has **no positive control** - nothing in it watches the detector fire, which is the gap step 80 closed for the POSIX scanner by shipping a fixture with the banned constructs in it; until that exists, this mutation is the only witness that the scan works. steps.title: Shipped .sh entry points are executable
steps.note: Reclassified under WQ-462 rather than retrofitted, because no mutation of this pack can make this step fail. Its subject is the git index - the only place the execute bit durably lives, since a folder copy, a zip and a Windows checkout all lose it - and the runner mutates file content. On this checkout the question is moot twice over: the pack keeps no version control by decision (WQ-459), so the step takes its documented [SKIP] on every run here and a skipped step cannot be proven able to fail. Its real proof is a git-backed clone on Linux or macOS, which is what pack-os-smoke.yml is for; see WQ-455.

steps.title: The path-key primitives answer, and answer differently (WQ-446)

mutation.why: Turns the segment test back into a substring test, which is the fault the primitive was written to end: a bare '__pycache__' also matches a file named __pycache__.txt, and '.git' swallows .gitignore. The damage runs the wrong way round from most defects - the filter gets broader, so scans quietly exclude files they are supposed to judge and every step downstream reports clean on a smaller tree than it claims to have read.

steps.note: The primitive is called by most scans in the suite, but a wider exclusion produces fewer findings rather than more, so collateral would show up as steps staying green - which is why step 63 tests the primitive directly with a file named after a directory rather than trusting its callers to notice.

steps.title: A bump moves current cites and never the Done log (WQ-437)

mutation.why: Drops the plural from the config key, so the declared regions load as none and the sync writes the whole file - including the Done log, whose rows are claims about which engine shipped each item. This is how the protection would really disappear: the key is read in one place, the typo is invisible in review, and the tool reports 'ok' while rewriting the past. Four historical cites were lost that way before WQ-437, twice in one session.
mutation.rejected: Iterating an empty list instead was rejected on the same reasoning as step 13: an obviously emptied loop reads as broken code, while a key that is one character off reads as working code and is what a maintainer would actually ship.

steps.note: Arm 4 is the witness, and it is the only arm that runs the tool: arms 1 to 3 read the config through verify-work-queue.ps1, which is PowerShell and still finds the declaration, and arm 5's backstop compares against git HEAD. So the mutation separates 'the config declares protection' from 'the tool honours it', which is the distinction the step was built for. The note this row used to carry - that a planted defect must be parse-checked - is satisfied by construction here, because the replacement is a string literal rather than a statement. Expect step 22 as collateral and read it as confirmation rather than noise: step 22 runs tests/test_pack_audit.py, whose test_version_sync_leaves_the_historical_region_alone asserts frozenRegions contains the work queue, so the same invariant is guarded twice - once as a unit test on the tool and once as a behavior arm on the config. A narrower mutation would have to break one of those and not the other, which would mean the two are no longer testing the same promise.

steps.title: Instructions name an entry point this host can run (WQ-449)

mutation.find: Write-Host "  5. Run $(Get-PackEntryPoint 'run_audit') after first test wiring"
mutation.replace: Write-Host "  5. Run run_audit.cmd after first test wiring"
mutation.why: Replaces a speller call with the Windows name it would have printed, in the closing instructions a reader gets after bootstrapping a project. On macOS or Linux the printed step is unrunnable as written, and nothing in the run says so - the script finished successfully and handed over a command that does not exist. Hardcoding what the speller already knows is the entire failure mode, and the site is a next-steps message because that is where it is most tempting.

steps.note: Proven the hard way first: writing the 2.22.99 semantic-report narrative put the host-write cmdlet's name on a line that already held two Windows entry points, and this step failed certification for it. The guard was right and the prose was changed. This spec makes the same point on purpose rather than by accident.

steps.title: A required POSIX twin has a delivery path (WQ-450)

mutation.why: Breaks the name the repair script writes while projectRequired keeps demanding run_tests.sh, producing unclearable drift: every audit of a POSIX project reports a missing required file, and the one tool that could create it writes a differently named one instead. A one-character rename is the honest shape here - the two lists are cross-checked rather than shared, precisely because a pair needs a template name that projectRequired cannot express, and cross-checked lists drift by typo.

steps.note: fourteen negative controls run step 66 own source against a planted copy
steps.rejected: First spec broke run_tests.sh and was inert - projectRequired does not demand that twin, so nothing was left undeliverable. The mistake surfaced something worth recording: arm 1's comment claims it checks both directions, but the loop only walks projectRequired asking whether each required twin is deliverable. The opposite direction it describes - a deliverable twin nobody requires - is not implemented, and run_tests.sh is a live instance of it. Harmless today, since the repair writes it either way, but the comment overstates the code.

steps.title: The documented POSIX start command runs at mode 644 (WQ-454)

mutation.why: Turns the numbered install step in the first file a consumer opens into the one form that cannot work. The execute bit is recorded by git and nothing else this pack travels through, so a folder copy, an unzipped archive and exFAT media all deliver mode 644 - and `./install.sh` exits 126 before printing anything a reader could act on, while `bash install.sh` runs a file at any mode. The command that repairs the missing bit is the command the missing bit stops.

steps.note: controls both ways: four instruction forms caught, five legal mentions spared

steps.title: No shipped doc calls the profile rules folder a load path (WQ-457)

mutation.why: Restores the false claim WQ-456 spent a release disproving: that a rule sitting in the profile folder reaches an agent. Flipping an existing disclaimer rather than adding a new sentence is the regression that actually happened - the claim came back in 2.22.80 in the one file written for users of other tools, after being corrected in about fifteen documents.

steps.note: five planted load claims must be caught, six correct mentions tolerated. Retrofit under WQ-462: the concern recorded in 2.22.86, that a spec cannot hold text another guard bans, does not bite here - step 68 scans .md, .mdc, .template and .txt, and this registry is .json. Two targets were rejected first. pack/docs/portable/GENERIC_RULES.md is generated, so mutating it fails the export-drift check alongside the step under test. The START_HERE.md row was worse - inert: replacing only its bolded negation leaves the cell label 'Rules, best-effort copy' on the same line, and the detector's disclaimer window tolerates it by design, so the suite stayed green and the mutation proved nothing. A load-claim mutation must remove every disclaimer word within one line either side of the claim, and that is easier to verify against the detector's own regexes than by reading.

steps.title: 'Is this a git work tree' is asked of git, not of the filesystem (WQ-461)

mutation.why: Reverts one call site from asking git to asking the filesystem, which is the original defect exactly: deleting a repository leaves a .git directory behind whenever an editor holds its index open, so Test-Path answers yes while git answers 'not a repository'. This checkout hit that an hour after being certified git-optional, and verify-work-queue.ps1 was one of the scripts that exited 1 because of it.

steps.note: expectations table with want=$true/$false; two positive controls need a real repo

steps.title: An inert always-on rule in the profile is reported, not trusted (WQ-460)

mutation.why: Inverts the orphan test, so the detector reports only rules the pack does ship and never the ones it does not - which is the state WQ-460 was found in, where no detection existed at all. An orphan is by definition absent from the install record, so this is also why -Prune cannot reach these files: both mechanisms end up looking for the orphan in the one list that cannot contain it.

steps.note: orphan detector controls plus an assertion that no step invokes doctor.ps1

steps.title: A step cannot be added without declaring how it is proven able to fail (WQ-443)

mutation.why: Renumbers the first registered step so the registry declares a step the suite never announces, and leaves step 1 undeclared. Both are the disagreement step 71 exists to catch, so a green suite under this mutation means step 71 is not reading anything. Chosen because it mutates the artifact the step guards rather than the step's own source - a step edited into passing proves nothing.

steps.note: First step added under the registry, and the first that could not be grandfathered: 71 is above the seal of 70. It also carries twelve in-process planted defects plus a positive control, which run on every suite run rather than only when the runner does.

steps.title: A failure is attributed to the step that raised it (WQ-443 Phase 3)

mutation.why: Makes Resolve-PackBehaviorStep answer nothing for every line. An always-null resolver is the failure mode that matters, because it would leave the mutation runner unable to name any step while every step still passed - a runner reporting success having observed nothing. Step 72's controls include lines that must resolve to a step, so this cannot pass.

steps.note: Attribution is taken from the call site rather than from output, because a planted control's child verify prints the same [FAIL] prefix. Verified on both PowerShell hosts, including a Fail raised inside a helper defined hundreds of lines earlier, which must be credited to the calling step.

steps.title: A mutation that changes nothing cannot pass as a proof (WQ-443 Phase 4)

mutation.why: Stops Get-PackMutationSpecProblem rejecting a find that matches zero times or twice. That is the runner's own silent-success mode: a stale spec would be applied as a no-op, the suite would stay green, and the green would be recorded as a proof. Step 73's controls include an absent find and a doubled find, so it cannot survive this.

steps.note: Tests the runner's two judgements in-process and asserts the runner actually uses them, rather than invoking the runner - the runner runs this suite, which is the recursion that killed step 70.

steps.title: A failing child's reason survives into the Fix line (WQ-463)

mutation.why: Makes the detail empty for every child, failing or not - which is the state WQ-463 was found in, where a parent reported that a verify failed and said nothing about why. The mutation is deliberately silent rather than noisy, because the defect it recreates was silent: the Fix line still appears, still names the right script, and simply carries no reason.

steps.note: Added above the seal, so grandfathering is not available to it - the reason this step arrived with a mutation rather than an exemption. Its last control asserts run_audit_core.ps1 actually calls the helper, because a tested function nobody uses reports nothing.

steps.title: Verification covers the pack under test and this machine's install, not backups (WQ-463)

mutation.why: Restores the behavior that caused WQ-463: verification accepting every pack copy discovery can find, so a backup on a Desktop or a removable disk is audited as though it were the pack under test. The mutation is the exact line that turns broad discovery into scoped verification.

steps.note: Discovery stays broad on purpose - a project outside the pack has to be able to find one. This step guards the narrower question verification asks. Its controls include path spelling, because a normalization miss would drop the real pack instead of a backup and verify nothing at all, which reads as success.

steps.title: Derived version cites are synced before they are checked (WQ-463)

mutation.why: Removes the sync from the test entry point, restoring the state WQ-463 was found in: an engine bump leaves AUDIT_SYSTEM.md on the old version, verify-audit-system fails on the mismatch, and the failure surfaces two layers away inside a generated project's bootstrap check before the audit's own later sync quietly repairs it.

steps.note: Guards order, not merely presence. A sync that runs after the check repairs the symptom for the next run and proves nothing about this one - which is exactly why the defect read as intermittent for six audit runs.

steps.title: The markdown section slicer has one home (WQ-444)

mutation.why: Removes the line anchor from the start-header search, restoring the 2.22.73 defect exactly: a heading quoted inside a table cell starts the section, so the Done log begins in the middle of the Active table and every Active id reads as both active and done. Mutating the behavior rather than the single-home check is deliberate - consolidating five copies of a broken function would satisfy a presence check and fix nothing.

steps.note: The single-home control scans every pack script for a private definition, because five byte-identical copies are how one defect cost five patches. The behavioral controls come first: one copy of the wrong thing is not an improvement.

steps.title: A generated project's runners delegate to one implementation (WQ-447)

mutation.why: Points the generated .sh entry point at an implementation the .bat does not use, which is the WQ-447 failure exactly: two platforms running different work, with the audit's test-pass proof covering only whichever one ran it. The comment above the exec line still cites the shared implementation, so this also confirms the step reads executable lines rather than prose.

steps.note: Judged on generated output, not on the templates, because reading a template is evidence about the template. The last control asserts the implementation is non-empty: two wrappers agreeing on nothing is not delegation. Expect step 23 as collateral, like step 46: any mutation of a runner template also reaches the generated projects step 23 bootstraps and runs, so there is no target that isolates this step.

steps.title: AGENTS.md may name the entry points this OS actually uses (WQ-452)

mutation.find: if not any(alt in text for alt in alternatives):
mutation.replace: if not all(alt in text for alt in alternatives):
mutation.why: Turns any-of back into all-of, restoring WQ-452: a project's AGENTS.md would have to name every platform's spelling of an entry point, so the Linux-facing document fails and so does the Windows-facing one. Chosen over deleting the default list because it leaves the shape intact and breaks only the judgement, which is what the step reads.

steps.note: Two of the four controls exist to stop the fix going too far: an AGENTS.md naming no entry point at all must still be caught, and a config that pins exact strings must still pin them. A permissive check that passes everything would satisfy the first two controls alone. The find is indented to twelve spaces on purpose - Section F carries the identical line at eight, and a spec matching twice is rejected. Expect step 23 as collateral: under all-of, the generated projects it bootstraps cannot name every platform's spelling either, so their audits fail too.

steps.title: Cited project paths are owned, and delivered ones are still deliverable (WQ-433)

mutation.why: Plants the original WQ-433 incident: a doc renames the file it cites and the cite is left pointing at nothing, so an agent told to read it first reads nothing. The undeclared default is the arm this reddens, which is the one that matters - it is what makes a new cite checked without anyone listing it. Chosen over mutating a declaration in the manifest because that would prove only that the checker reads its own list.
mutation.rejected: Deleting pack/templates/docs/ROADMAP.md.template would exercise the deliverable arm with a real defect - advice to keep a roadmap that no template writes - but bootstrap copies that template, so steps 23, 33, 34 and 78 would all go red and four failing steps prove less than one.

steps.note: The arms split three ways on purpose, because only one of the three owners is checkable by asking whether the file is here. Extraction is tested in memory (a backslash cite is the same path, `.md.template` must not truncate to `.md`, and a pack/-rooted cite belongs to step 47); the judgement is tested against a synthetic tree with six planted defects including a stale exemption; and the live arm requires at least 100 cites, since a scan that finds nothing passes for the same reason a blinded one does. The reader-owned exemptions print as INFO every run: an indiscriminate pass over these three roots reports 68 correct-but-irrelevant findings, which is how the first attempt got muted, and the answer is an enumerated list rather than a quieter check.

steps.title: A passing run must not print a [FAIL] line (WQ-472)

mutation.why: Inverts the gate on Get-PackStrayFailureLine, so the helper answers about failing runs and says nothing about passing ones. That is the defect in its purest form: the leak detector goes quiet exactly where a leak can happen, and the parent audit keeps quoting fixture findings as its own. It reddens the step through two arms rather than one - the leaked line is not reported, and a real failure has its own lines reported as strays - which is the right shape for a check whose whole value is knowing which side of the exit code it is on.
mutation.rejected: Reverting step 57's absolute-path arm to an error-only redirect would reproduce the original incident exactly, but the invariant is enforced by the parent, and no step runs verify-audit-system against this suite: step 23 passes -SkipBehavior and step 73 exists to keep that recursion out. The source-shape arm would catch it, and a mutation proven by a grep is weaker than one proven by behaviour.

steps.note: The invariant belongs to the parent, not to any one arm: a run that exited 0 must not have printed a marked failure line. It is tested here on fixtures because the parent that enforces it cannot be run from inside this suite. Three arms cover the sides an exit-code gate can get wrong (clean pass, passing leak, real failure), one covers a single captured string with a blank line in it, and two ask whether the parent still keeps a copy of the output and still calls the helper. The source-shape arm is the early-warning half: the invariant fires once a leak exists, the grep fires when one is written.

steps.title: The offload hooks decide, not merely exist (WQ-476)

mutation.why: Points the detector at a heading no message carries, so it finds no ask section and flags nothing. This is the failure mode the control exists to prevent and the one that cannot be seen by reading: the hook still parses its payload, still reads the shared list, still writes its log, still exits 0 - and silently approves every offload. It is the same shape as the BOM defect that made the first live version of shell-preapprove.ps1 a no-op while looking installed, which is why this step executes the hooks instead of grepping them.
mutation.rejected: Deleting a hook file, or emptying the neutral policy, would also redden the step - but through the inventory and list-sharing arms, which prove only that files exist. A mutation that survives the arms it is aimed at and fails somewhere cheaper is a mutation that measures the wrong thing. Inverting the refuse-list loop in shell-preapprove.ps1 was the other candidate and reddens one arm; this one reddens the detector's whole purpose.

steps.note: Runs the shipped hooks rather than reading them, with every payload BOM-prefixed the way Cursor sends them - a hook that cannot read past U+FEFF is a no-op, and one shipped in that state for four commands before anyone noticed. Arms: file inventory; the template's deliberate asymmetry (the two tightening hooks registered with a loop cap, pre-approval left off because widening unattended execution is a project owner's call); the detector flagging an ask that names a pre-approved command, with reason, evidence and generation id; the two discrimination cases that decide whether anyone leaves this enabled (an ask to run install.ps1 is the human's, and prose naming commands is not an ask); the gate's silence with no verdict, its handback with one, its consumption of the flag, and its refusal of both a stale generation and a second loop; the approver allowing a verify gate while refusing a profile write and a chained command; and that every adapter decides from one host-neutral policy rather than a private copy. WQ-480 added the portability arms: that the policy is authored in globs (the direction that compiles losslessly to a regex host and a glob host both, unlike the regex it started as), that it compiles to OpenCode's permission.bash map with refuse becoming ask rather than deny, and that bootstrap both delivers the policy outside .cursor/ and compiles it into opencode.json. The hooks run from a STAGED project tree, not from where they ship, so the upward walk that finds .agent-control/policy.json is exercised rather than the fallback. All of it under a probe LOCALAPPDATA so the real flag and logs are never touched.

steps.title: StarterPack-Airlock discovery and refresh overlay merge (WQ-487)

The step's refresh arm expects starterPackAirlockActive and overlay paths in requiredReads; without discovery both stay empty and the arm fails.
mutation.rejected: Mutating Find-StarterPackAirlock in pack-paths.ps1 would redden every consumer and every simulate scenario, not just refresh. The defect under test is specifically whether refresh wires discovery into requiredReads.

steps.note: Mirrors simulate scenarios S01-S04 on Find-StarterPackAirlock (null without folder, valid layout resolves, wrong key and missing key fail closed), then runs refresh-agent-context.ps1 with -StarterPackAirlockDesktopRoots under an isolated AGENT_STARTER_PACK_STATE_ROOT. Active Airlock must set starterPackAirlockActive, record overlayRequiredReads, append overlay paths to requiredReads, and still list the working-copy docs/WORK_QUEUE.md. Inactive desktop must leave overlay fields empty.

steps.title: Recurring audit sync drift names a live writer (WQ-481)

mutation.why: Blinds recurring-drift detection so a second verify-only run on the same installed path reports only the generic sync advice. Step 85 runs verify twice on unchanged drift and requires [RECURRING DRIFT] on the second pass.

steps.note: Static read for [RECURRING DRIFT] and guard-proofs.lock, then a miniature packMirror probe under AGENT_STARTER_PACK_INSTALL_ROOT and AGENT_STARTER_PACK_STATE_ROOT: first verify records drift, second verify on unchanged drift must print recurring guidance, sync plus clean verify must clear session state.

steps.title: Dual-zone Airlock publish gate (WQ-488)

mutation.why: Removes the distinct dual-zone failure banner when Zone A passed but Zone B failed. Step 86's VERSION-drift arm still fails via B09 sync, but the static read requires [DUAL-ZONE FAIL] in the gate script.
